stem: A 33-year-old man had a transsphenoidal resection of a large pituitary adenoma 1 year ago. He has low libido and infertility. Testosterone is 90 ng/dL (low), LH and FSH are undetectable, and semen analysis shows azoospermia. He wants to have a child.
oneliner: 33M + pituitary adenoma resected 1 y ago + low libido, infertility + low testosterone, undetectable LH and FSH + azoospermia + wants fertility → which drug?
ask: Which of the following is most appropriate to restore spermatogenesis?

whyNot.A: The **pituitary is damaged**, so it cannot respond to GnRH
whyNot.B: Works through the **hypothalamic-pituitary axis**, which is not functioning

answer: hCG (acts like LH) plus FSH injections
why: **Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism after pituitary surgery.** The pituitary cannot respond to GnRH or clomiphene. **hCG acts like LH** on Leydig cells and **FSH** drives Sertoli cells, restoring sperm production.

drug.name: hCG (with FSH)
drug.how: hCG mimics LH at Leydig cells; FSH stimulates Sertoli cells and spermatogenesis
drug.use: Male hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with infertility, ovulation induction, cryptorchidism
drug.watch: Gynecomastia, injection-site reactions, ovarian hyperstimulation (women); testosterone alone lowers sperm count

stem: A 24-year-old woman has had amenorrhea for 6 months and bilateral milky nipple discharge. Pregnancy test and TSH are normal, and she takes no medications. Prolactin is 200 ng/mL, and MRI shows an 8-mm lesion in the pituitary with no extension toward the optic chiasm.
oneliner: 24F + amenorrhea 6 mo + milky discharge + normal pregnancy test and TSH + no medications + prolactin 200 + 8-mm pituitary lesion → which drug?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

whyNot.B: **5-HT1B/D agonist** for migraine; no effect on prolactin
whyNot.C: **Somatostatin analog**: used for acromegaly, not prolactinoma
whyNot.E: Causes **milk ejection** and uterine contraction; does not lower prolactin

why: **Prolactin 200 with a pituitary microadenoma** = prolactinoma. First-line treatment is a **dopamine agonist** (cabergoline or bromocriptine) that lowers prolactin and shrinks the tumor.

drug.name: Cabergoline (also bromocriptine)
drug.how: Stimulates D2 receptors on lactotrophs, lowering prolactin and tumor size
drug.watch: Nausea, orthostatic hypotension, psychiatric effects; valvular fibrosis at high doses

stem: A 13-year-old boy has had 3 weeks of thirst, frequent urination and a 6 kg weight loss. Glucose is 410 mg/dL and urine ketones are positive. C-peptide is low and anti-GAD antibodies are present. His parents hope he can be treated with tablets.
oneliner: 13M + 3 weeks thirst, polyuria, 6 kg weight loss + glucose 410 + urine ketones positive + low C-peptide + anti-GAD antibodies + parents hope for tablets → most appropriate drug?
ask: Which drug should be prescribed for his diabetes?

whyNot.A: Releases insulin only from working beta cells, and his **C-peptide is low**
whyNot.B: Does not replace missing insulin; he has **ketones and low C-peptide**
whyNot.C: Raises insulin release from beta cells, but his **C-peptide is low**
whyNot.E: Improves insulin sensitivity but needs insulin to work; his **C-peptide is low** and he is ketotic

why: **Young age, weight loss, ketones, low C-peptide and anti-GAD antibodies** mean type 1 diabetes with autoimmune loss of beta cells. Sulfonylureas, gliptins and other oral drugs need **working beta cells** or residual insulin, so only **insulin** is adequate.

drug.name: Insulin
drug.how: Binds the insulin receptor (tyrosine kinase) to move glucose into muscle and fat via GLUT4, promote glycogen and fat storage, and suppress hepatic glucose output and lipolysis
drug.use: Type 1 diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, advanced type 2 diabetes, gestational diabetes, hyperkalemia
drug.watch: Hypoglycemia; weight gain; hypokalemia; injection-site lipohypertrophy

idea.rule: Drugs that stimulate insulin release or improve its action fail when the beta cells are gone.
also: Sulfonylureas and meglitinides: close K-ATP channels in beta cells
GLP-1 agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors: glucose-dependent insulin release
Metformin and pioglitazone: sensitize tissues to insulin
Type 1 diabetes: insulin is the only effective treatment
